citation.title: Multi-material Multi-physics Topology Optimization with Physics-informed Gaussian Process Priors
citation.authors: Xiangyu Sun, Shirin Hosseinmardi, Amin Yousefpour, and Ramin Bostanabad
citation.venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: For 2D mass-only cases, PIGP median compliance was 1.049, 0.976, 1.133, and 3.529 across four examples, compared with ordered SIMP values 0.982, 0.890, 1.041, and 3.194.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: No classical-method speed-up factor is reported; the conclusion says training costs are higher than SIMP.
claim.alternatives: The conclusion says PIGP has higher training costs than SIMP and that COMSOL is slower; neither is quantified.

baseline.classical_method: Ordered SIMP; PolyMat; 3D SIMP; COMSOL for thermo-mechanical cases
baseline.hardware_classical: Intel Core i7-11700K CPU (Section 4, numerical setup)
baseline.problem_size: 2D and 3D examples; FE node counts in Table 3; thermo-mechanical grids in Table 14
baseline.training_time: not stated; up to 10,000 epochs, and 20,000 for thermo-mechanical case (Sections 4 setup, 4.3)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; no offline training dataset described
baseline.quality_metric: FEM compliance/objective and mass or cost constraints (Tables 4, 5, 15)
baseline.quality_gap: Described as comparable; Table 4 gives medians across 10 runs and Table 5 reports compliance and mass statistics.

R1.evidence: Section 5, Conclusions: primary comparison concerns objective quality; speed is not the primary outcome.

R2.evidence: Section 4 setup identifies CPU and GPU classes but establishes no R2 criterion about baseline efficiency.

R3.evidence: Sections 3–4 describe per-problem optimization; no offline model training dataset or amortized query claim is stated.

R4.evidence: Sections 4.1–4.3 and Tables 4, 5, 15 evaluate final designs by FEM and report constraint values; Section 4.3 notes disconnected features but no failure rate is reported.

reporting.n_test_cases: Four 2D and four 3D compliance examples; heat conduction, compliant mechanism, and thermo-mechanical examples (Sections 4.1–4.3).

notes: Section 4 states each experiment was repeated 10 times and final objectives were evaluated by FEM. Replication statement says model code is accessible via GitHub upon publication; public availability is not established in the article text.
